 Exclusive: 16-yr Census gap forced India’s welfare framework to ‘operate on shadows’—Ex-census chief
 From food entitlements to schools & hospitals, India’s planning relies on population data from 2011. Census delay has created a statistical blind spot, warns ex-Census chief Chandramouli in new book.
 Moushumi Das Gupta

 New Delhi:  The 16-year gap in conducting the Indian Census—the last one was conducted in 2011—will remain a “permanent scar in India’s statistical record”, forcing Indian planners, policymakers and researchers to work with projections that risk becoming “dangerously detached from reality”, Dr C. Chandramouli, India’s former Census Commissioner and Registrar General of India has written in his new book, ‘Counting a Nation: The Story of the Indian Census’.
 Published by Macmillan, the yet to be released book comes barely two months before the Population Enumeration, the second and penultimate phase of Census 2027 which starts across the country on 10 January 2027.
 Chandramouli led the 2011 Census and piloted the National Population Register and the Socio Economic and Caste Census as India’s Registrar General and Census Commissioner between November 2009 and July 2015.
 Show Full Article
 After 2011, the next Census was due in 2021 but it was postponed because of the Covid-19 pandemic. What was supposed to be a “temporary delay” had dragged on for 16 years.
 Chandramouli, a 1985 batch Tamil Nadu cadre IAS officer, who retired as DoPT secretary in September 2020 writes that a 16-year absence is not merely an “administrative delay”, it is an “epistemic void”.
 “Without regular enumeration, the state loses sight of itself. Budgets for schools and hospitals rely on decade-old figures; urban planning proceeds on outdated assumptions; poverty estimates drift without anchors; and the architecture of welfare is forced to operate on shadows rather than people,” the former Census Commissioner writes.
 In a scathing indictment of the consequences of the delay, Chandramouli further writes, “A democracy cannot govern what it cannot see, and India—for the first time in independent history—is navigating without a current demographic compass.”
 Dr C. Chandramouli’s new book | By special arrangement 
 Implications of the delay 
 According to the former Census Commissioner, the “gravest impact” of the census delay was on welfare delivery.
 “The census is the backbone of India’s welfare state, providing the population shares and household counts that determine the scope of schemes. With outdated numbers, welfare becomes mis-targeted: Millions are excluded while others are wrongly included,” Chandramouli writes.
 The National Food Security Act 2013 that entitles 67 percent of India’s population to subsidised foodgrains also faced the brunt of the delayed census after 2011. “In 2011, 81.35 crore people were covered. By 2023, India’s population had grown by over 200 million, yet the beneficiary cap had not been updated. This means an estimated 100 million eligible poor people may be excluded from food entitlements simply because the census has not been updated,” he writes.
 Chandramouli writes that the impact of the delay has been felt across the board, be it figuring out India’s official population to migration data, fertility transition, housing, education and health.
 For instance, by 2023, the UN estimated India’s population would be at 1.43 billion, overtaking China and making it the world’s most populous nation. “But without census confirmation, these remain modelled estimates. How many children are being born, where exactly growth is concentrated and how age structures are shifting—all remain uncertain,” he writes.
 Similarly, planning for schools, anganwadis and Primary Health Centres (PHCs) depends on knowing how many children exist in each locality. “With no census update, many districts are either under-served or misallocated,” he writes.
 The irony, according to Chandramouli, is stark. “…at a time when India has dramatically expanded its welfare architecture—from food and housing to toilets, bank accounts and health insurance—the foundational dataset for targeting these programmes remain frozen in 2011,” he writes.
 Indian census data, Chandramouli writes, has long been admired by international agencies such as the UN Population Division, World Bank and International Monetary Fund, which depended heavily on it for global datasets. But the census gap has dented that reputation.
 “Comparable global reports now have to rely on projections rather than hard data… India risks being seen as a statistical laggard even as it positions itself as a global leader. As the only democracy of its scale to break the census rhythm, India’s credibility as a data-rich society is at stake,” he writes.
 (Edited by Viny Mishra)
